what_it_does: Zero-knowledge proofs are a cryptographic technique that lets one party prove to another that a statement is true (for example, 'I know the solution to this puzzle') without revealing anything else — a key building block in privacy-preserving blockchains and secure computation. Generating such proofs requires a mathematical operation called the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), which is similar to the Fourier transform that processes audio or images but works with integers. NTT is slow enough to be the main bottleneck in proof generation, and the obvious fix — spreading the work across many GPUs — backfires because the algorithm requires shuffling large amounts of data between GPUs in a pattern that generates more communication than a single GPU can handle. This paper restructures the NTT algorithm so that data-shuffling steps are batched together and timed to overlap with computation, and assigns work to GPUs in a way that matches the actual physical wiring between them to maximize the bandwidth used.
